title: Word forms from a table, not rules
statement: Decide in code whether words are forms of the same word by looking them up in a published table of word forms, never by spelling rules.
example: A suffix-trimmer that did it by rule gave 234 false unfamiliar-word candidates across 25 lesson runs.
detail: A content audit for Grade 3 reading lessons asks whether two words are the same word in several checks, from an answer that echoes the question to whether a word is familiar at the grade. The suffix-trimmer it first used missed every irregular form, giving 234 false unfamiliar-word candidates across 25 lesson runs, and invented links such as bees to "be" and manner to "man" (`shadow/content-eval/SKILL.md`). It now looks words up in a published lemmatization list and in WordNet's derivation links, and a missing form is added as a line in the table, not as a rule.
against: The tables have limits: "- A word the tables don't list matches only itself." (`shadow/content-eval/SKILL.md`, line 146), and an ambiguous form joins both of its families.

evidence.quote: **Word forms come from published tables, never from suffix rules.**
The suffix-trimmer this replaced missed every irregular form: 234 false unfamiliar-word candidates across the 25 lesson runs (chose ×9, given, forgotten, teeth, mice).
It also invented links such as bees → "be", manner → "man" and stared → "star".
- To add a missing form, append a line to the table. Don't add a rule.
